definitions.definition: The instrument of valid cognition; four: perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony (NS 1.1.3). That by which the knower knows; purposeful because it makes action succeed (NBh 1.1.1).
Two only: perception and inference, verbal knowledge being explained as inference (VS 9.18–19 in Candrānanda's recension; Praśastapāda).
The special cause (karaṇa) of a valid cognition; the four khaṇḍas of the Tattvacintāmaṇi follow the four means.

The twelve objects whose true knowledge leads to liberation: self, body, senses, objects, cognition, mind, activity, faults, rebirth, fruit, pain, liberation (NS 1.1.9); other objects (the Vaiśeṣika categories) are acknowledged (NBh 1.1.9).
Deliberation awaiting a distinguishing mark (NS 1.1.23); a cognition of one thing as qualified by mutually opposed properties, e.g. 'a post or a man?' (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The aim with regard to which one acts (NS 1.1.24).
A thing about which ordinary people and critical examiners agree (NS 1.1.25).
A settled position; four kinds: common to all systems, peculiar to one, implied, and provisionally accepted (NS 1.1.26–31).
(1) A member of the demonstrative statement — proposition, reason, example, application, conclusion (NS 1.1.32); (2) a part of a whole.
A part, in which the whole (avayavin) inheres.
Reasoned consideration of what fits, about a thing whose nature is unknown (NS 1.1.40); neither a means of knowledge nor included among them, but their helper (NBh 1.1.1).
Superimposition of the pervader through superimposing the pervaded ('if there were no fire there would be no smoke'); classed as a non-valid cognition that assists (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Determination of a thing after deliberation by thesis and counter-thesis (NS 1.1.41).

Debate in which both sides prove and refute with the means of knowledge and tarka, without contradicting tenets, using the five members (NS 1.2.1); undertaken with teachers, pupils and seekers of the good (NS 4.2.48).
Debate with the features of vāda in which quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat are also used (NS 1.2.2); permitted to protect the ascertainment of truth (NS 4.2.50).
Wrangling without establishing a counter-thesis (NS 1.2.3); the caviller who states a purpose thereby adopts a thesis (NBh 1.1.1).
Debate as a genre, of three kinds: vāda, jalpa and vitaṇḍā.
A reason that only appears to be one; five in the sūtra: inconclusive, contradictory, prakaraṇasama, sādhyasama, kālātīta (NS 1.2.4).
Five in the Navya list: inconclusive, contradictory, counterbalanced, unestablished, sublated (Tarkasaṅgraha); defined generally in the Tattvacintāmaṇi's hetvābhāsa-sāmānya-nirukti.
Countering a statement by supposing an alternative meaning; verbal, generalizing and figurative (NS 1.2.10–17).

(1) In debate: a futile rejoinder based merely on similarity or dissimilarity (NS 1.2.18), of twenty-four kinds (NS 5.1.1). (2) The universal, 'that whose nature is to produce sameness' (NS 2.2.71), part of a word's meaning (NS 2.2.68).
The universal (synonym of sāmānya), e.g. substance-hood; genuine universals are limited by six impediments (Udayana).

notes: Homonym: other units define jāti as birth or social class.

definitions.definition: Occasion for rebuke in debate: misunderstanding or non-understanding (NS 1.2.19); twenty-two kinds (NS 5.2.1).
Cognition arising from sense-object contact, non-verbalizable, non-deviating, determinate (NS 1.1.4).
Arises from the contact of self, sense, mind and object (VS 3.1.13, 9.15 Candrānanda); includes yogic perception (VS 9.13).
Cognition produced by sense-object contact, indeterminate or determinate, through six contacts; also extraordinary (alaukika) perception.
Knowledge preceded by perception, of three kinds (NS 1.1.5); resting on perception and scripture it is anvīkṣā (NBh 1.1.1).
Knowledge from a mark (laiṅgika): effect, cause, connected, co-inherent, opposed (VS 9.18); includes verbal knowledge.
The instrument of inferential cognition, i.e. consideration (parāmarśa); for oneself or for others.
Establishing what is to be established through similarity to the well known (NS 1.1.6).
Yields knowledge of the name–named relation from cognition of similarity (the gavaya example).
Not a separate means; included in inference (Praśastapāda).
(1) Verbal testimony: the instruction of a reliable person (NS 1.1.7), of seen or unseen objects (NS 1.1.8). (2) Sound, the object of hearing and a non-eternal quality of ākāśa (NS 1.1.14, 2.2.13).
Sound: a quality of ākāśa, its mark, produced by conjunction, disjunction and sound, non-eternal (VS 2.1.24–27, 2.2.36–37 Candrānanda); verbal knowledge is inference (VS 9.19).
Verbal testimony is a statement produced by true knowledge of the meaning that causes its utterance (Tattvacintāmaṇi); sound is of two kinds, inarticulate and phonemic (Tarkasaṅgraha).

One who has directly experienced the thing and speaks from the wish to communicate it as seen — the same definition for seers, āryas and mlecchas (NBh 1.1.7); the Veda is valid because its seers and teachers are reliable (NS 2.1.69).
One who speaks of things as they are (yathārthavaktā) (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Experience that apprehends, in what has a property, that property as its qualifier (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Correct determination (Udayana, NK 4.5).
The one who acts, impelled by the wish to obtain or avoid, and who knows through a means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1).
The knowing that results from a means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1); it culminates in perception (NBh 1.1.3).
Validity of a cognition, known extrinsically (parataḥ).
Produced by excellences in the causes and known by inference, not by the cognition that apprehends the cognition (Prāmāṇyavāda).
The Nyāya theory of error: a thing is cognized as qualified by a property it lacks — the silver seen elsewhere is presented in the mother-of-pearl.
False cognition, e.g. 'this is silver' of mother-of-pearl (Tarkasaṅgraha).
One of the forms of non-knowledge (avidyā) (Praśastapāda).
A mental perception, following a cognition, of the form 'I know this'; the means by which a cognition is known, since a cognition does not reveal itself.
A determinate cognition; 'vyavasāyātmaka' in NS 1.1.4 denotes determinate perception (Vācaspati).
Perception without a qualifier ('this is something'); read by Vācaspati into 'avyapadeśya' in NS 1.1.4.
Not itself perceived but inferred as the first stage of determinate perception.
Perception with a qualifier, e.g. 'this is Ḍittha, a brāhmaṇa, dark' (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The contact of sense and object from which perception arises (NS 1.1.4); six kinds (Uddyotakara).
Six ordinary contacts plus three extraordinary ones.

Perception through an extraordinary contact: through the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇā — grasping all smoke via smoke-hood, which grounds pervasion), through a prior cognition (jñānalakṣaṇā — e.g. 'fragrant sandal' seen), and yogic (yogaja).
Perception of the self and other substances from a special conjunction of self and mind (VS 9.13–14); of yogins in concentration (yukta) and out of it (viyukta) (Praśastapāda).
The perception of one engaged in yoga arises from samādhi (NBh 1.1.3).
Yogaja, one of the three extraordinary contacts.
The rule of co-presence 'wherever there is smoke there is fire' (Tarkasaṅgraha); defined precisely after rejecting five provisional definitions (Tattvacintāmaṇi).
The relation between mark and marked on which inference rests (term prominent from Uddyotakara and Vācaspati on).
Cognition of the probans as qualified by pervasion and present in the subject ('this mountain has smoke pervaded by fire'), the instrument of inference.
A mark from which something is known; desire and the rest are marks of the self (NS 1.1.10).
Mark; synonymous with hetu, apadeśa, nimitta, pramāṇa, kāraṇa (VS 9.20 Candrānanda).
Three kinds: with positive and negative concomitance, positive only, negative only.
That in which the probandum is doubted, e.g. the mountain (Tarkasaṅgraha).
A side or thesis in debate (NS 1.1.41, 1.2.1).
What certainly possesses the probandum, e.g. the kitchen.
What certainly lacks the probandum, e.g. the lake.
Absence of certainty (of the probandum in the subject) not accompanied by a desire to infer.

literal: presence of the probans in the subject

definitions.definition: The probans's occurring in the mountain etc.

literal: probandum; what is to be proved

definitions.definition: What is to be proved, stated in the proposition (NS 1.1.33).
The member that proves what is to be proved by similarity or dissimilarity to the example (NS 1.1.34–35).
What pervades the probandum without pervading the probans (e.g. contact with wet fuel when smoke is inferred from fire); its presence makes the reason unestablished as to pervasion.
A probans or probandum with only positive concomitance, as 'knowable' or 'nameable', which has no absence anywhere; a test case for definitions of pervasion.
A probans with only negative concomitance, e.g. 'earth differs from the rest because it has smell'.
A probans with both positive and negative concomitance, e.g. smoke for fire.
Inference in one's own mind, from having grasped pervasion by repeated observation and then seeing the mark.
The five-membered statement by which one who has inferred makes another infer.
The statement of what is to be proved (NS 1.1.33).
The familiar instance possessing the property to be proved, or its opposite (NS 1.1.36–37).
Restating the subject as 'so' or 'not so' with reference to the example (NS 1.1.38).
Repeating the proposition on the ground of the reason (NS 1.1.39).

literal: like the prior (inference from cause, or from what was before)

definitions.definition: One of the three kinds of inference named in NS 1.1.5; the Bhāṣya offers more than one explanation.

literal: like the remainder (inference from effect, or by elimination)

definitions.definition: One of the three kinds of inference named in NS 1.1.5; the Bhāṣya offers more than one explanation.

literal: seen in general (inference from general correlation)

definitions.definition: One of the three kinds of inference named in NS 1.1.5; the Bhāṣya offers more than one explanation.
A Vedic statement that enjoins (NS 2.1.64 DCS).
Vedic statements of praise, blame, another's practice and ancient precedent (NS 2.1.65 DCS).
Repetition of what has been enjoined, distinct from mere repetition (NS 2.1.66–68 DCS).
Proposed as a means of knowledge; not different from verbal testimony (NS 2.2.2).
Proposed as a means of knowledge; included in inference (NS 2.2.2).
Included in inference (Praśastapāda).
Proposed as a means of knowledge (e.g. a thousand includes a hundred); included in inference (NS 2.2.2).
Proposed (as 'abhāva') as a separate means of knowledge; not different from inference (NS 2.2.2); later, absence is perceived through the qualifier-relation contact.
The cognition of a sentence-meaning produced by words, given expectancy, compatibility, proximity and known intention.

The denotative power of a word, which is the Lord's convention 'from this word this meaning is to be understood' (Tarkasaṅgraha); causal power as a separate category is rejected, efficacy being explained by the totality of causes and the absence of counteragents.

notes: Homonym: Śākta and Śaiva units define śakti as divine power.

definitions.definition: Lakṣaṇa: the distinguishing property by which what has been named is set apart from others — the second of the three activities of the śāstra (NBh 1.1.3).
Lakṣaṇā: secondary signification, when the primary meaning does not fit (e.g. 'the village on the Ganges').
Naming the things to be examined — the first activity of the śāstra (NBh 1.1.3).
Testing by the means of knowledge whether a definition fits — the third activity of the śāstra (NBh 1.1.3).
A word's inability to produce a connected cognition without another word (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Non-contradiction of the meaning ('sprinkle with fire' lacks it).
Uttering the words without delay.
The speaker's intention, knowledge of which is a condition of verbal cognition (Tātparyavāda).
Sounds ending in a case-ending (NS 2.2.60 DCS); its meaning is individual, form and universal (NS 2.2.68).
What possesses denotative power (Tarkasaṅgraha).
A group of words (Tarkasaṅgraha); Vedic sentences are valid as spoken by the Lord, worldly ones when spoken by a reliable person.
The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by understanding (VS 6.1.1).
A concrete thing that is the substrate of particular qualities (NS 2.2.69 DCS).
What is called the mark of the universal (NS 2.2.70 DCS).
The categories: substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence (six), with absence as seventh in later works.
The sixteen topics of NS 1.1.1; also 'word-meaning' (NS 2.2.68).
Seven categories (Tarkasaṅgraha, Bhāṣāpariccheda); Raghunātha re-examines the list.
What possesses motion and qualities and is an inherent cause (VS 1.1.14 C); nine (VS 1.1.4 C).
What resides in a substance, has no qualities and is not an independent cause of conjunction and disjunction (VS 1.1.15 C); twenty-four (Praśastapāda).

notes: Distinct from the Sāṃkhya sense (the three constituents of prakṛti).

definitions.definition: Motion: residing in one substance, without qualities, the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction (VS 1.1.16 C); five kinds (VS 1.1.6).
Action whose results bind; the body arises from the fruits of past actions (NS 3.2.60); 'activity' (pravṛtti) of speech, mind and body (NS 1.1.17).
Relative to cognition (VS 1.2.3 C); highest is being; eternal, one, present in many (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Residing in eternal substances and distinguishing them from one another; endless in number (Tarkasaṅgraha).
That from which the notion 'here' arises regarding effect and cause (VS 7.2.29 C); one eternal relation of inseparables (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The seventh category, of four kinds (prior, posterior, absolute, mutual); not listed by Praśastapāda because determined through its counterpositive, not because unreal (Udayana).
Proposed as a means of knowledge (in the sense of non-apprehension); reduced to inference (NS 2.2.2).
Absence of a product before it arises: beginningless, with an end; an effect is defined as the counterpositive of a prior absence.
Absence after destruction: with a beginning, without end.
Absence whose counterpositive is delimited by a relation for all three times ('no pot on the ground').
Absence whose counterpositive is delimited by identity ('a pot is not cloth').
The highest universal, distinct from substance, quality and motion, in which the notion 'existent' arises (VS 1.2.7–8 C).
The eternal, partless, imperceptible ultimate constituent of earth, water, fire and air; of spherical size (VS 4.1.1, 4.1.7, 7.1.26 C).
Division ends in atoms, which lie beyond the truṭi (NS 4.2.16–17); atoms are imperceptible (NS 2.1.37).

equivalents.note: Jain atoms are also partless and eternal but are undifferentiated as to element; the Vaiśeṣika holds four kinds of atoms.

definitions.definition: The product of two atoms, still imperceptible; through dyads and so on the gross elements arise (Praśastapāda).

literal: triad; the mote in a sunbeam

definitions.definition: The product of (three) dyads, the smallest visible substance — the mote seen in a sunbeam (later manuals).

notes: The 'three dyads' formula is from later manuals (recalled).

definitions.definition: The minimal, eternal magnitude of atoms (VS 7.1.26 C).
Substance possessing smell (with colour, taste, touch); eternal as atoms, non-eternal as products; our bodies are earthy.
Substance with cold touch, fluid and viscid; bodies of water in Varuṇa's world.
Substance with hot touch and colour; bodies of fire in Āditya's world; includes gold (mineral fire).
Substance with touch and without colour, inferred from touch; within the body it is breath.
One, all-pervading, eternal substance whose quality is sound.
One, all-pervading, eternal substance, cause of the notions 'earlier', 'later', 'simultaneous', 'quick' (VS 2.2.6 C).
One, all-pervading, eternal substance, cause of the notion 'this (is) from here' and of directions (VS 2.2.12 C).

An eternal substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition, known by the marks desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition (NS 1.1.10); the knower, the one who remembers (NS 3.2.40).
An all-pervading substance marked by breath, eye-movements, life, mind's movement, desire, effort etc. (VS 3.2.4 C); many (VS 3.2.16 C); perceived by yogins (VS 9.13).
The substrate of cognition; two kinds: the supreme self (the one omniscient Lord) and the individual self, distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
One in each body and atomic; its mark is the non-simultaneity of cognitions (NS 1.1.16, 3.2.56, 3.2.59).
An eternal atomic substance; its mark is the presence or absence of cognition when self, sense and object are in contact (VS 3.2.1, 7.1.30 C).
The inner sense, instrument of apprehending pleasure etc.; endless in number, atomic, eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Not different from apprehension and knowledge (NS 1.1.15); a non-eternal quality of the self, not an eternal inner instrument (against Sāṃkhya, NS 3.2.1–9).
The cause of all usage; memory or experience (Tarkasaṅgraha).

notes: Distinct from the Sāṃkhya-Yoga buddhi (mahat), a principle of prakṛti.

definitions.definition: Synonym of buddhi (NS 1.1.15); a mark and quality of the self (NS 1.1.10), not of the mind (NS 3.2.19).
A mark and special quality of the self (NS 1.1.10); 'desire is wanting' (Tarkasaṅgraha); eternal in the Lord.
A mark and special quality of the self; as a fault, one of the three groups (NS 4.1.3); 'aversion is anger' (Tarkasaṅgraha).
A mark and special quality of the self; eternal in the Lord (Tarkasaṅgraha).
What all experience as agreeable; a quality of the self; bound up with pain and so to be relinquished like food mixed with poison (NBh 1.1.2).
Characterized by affliction (NS 1.1.21); twenty-one kinds (Vācaspati); its absolute cessation is liberation.

That from which prosperity and the highest good result (VS 1.1.2); a quality of the self produced by enjoined acts (Tarkasaṅgraha); the knowledge of the categories arises from dharma manifested by the Lord's command (Praśastapāda).
A quality of the self produced by forbidden acts (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The unseen cause of motions without visible cause and of the mind's passage at death and birth; its absence is liberation (VS 5.1.15, 5.2.14, 5.2.19–20 C).
The residue of past action that brings about the body (NS 3.2.60); set in motion by the Lord (NBh 4.1.21).

equivalents.note: Mīmāṃsā's apūrva is the unseen potency produced by a rite; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika's adṛṣṭa is merit/demerit as qualities of the self — both link act to later result.

definitions.definition: A quality of three kinds: momentum, memory-impression and elasticity (Tarkasaṅgraha); memory arises from self–mind conjunction and impressions (VS 9.22 C).
The impression produced by experience that causes memory; resides only in the self (Tarkasaṅgraha).

notes: Homonym: in Buddhist and yoga contexts bhāvanā means cultivation / meditation.

definitions.definition: The impression that keeps a moving thing moving (Tarkasaṅgraha; VS 5.1.17 C on the arrow).
The impression that restores a thing (e.g. a mat) to its former state.
Non-inherent cause of the first falling; in earth and water.
Cause of the first flowing; natural in water, occasioned (by fire) in earth (ghee) and fire (gold).
Cause of the cohering of powder etc.; in water only.
Cause of measuring; four kinds: minute, large, long, short.
Cause of the usage 'separate'; in all substances.
Cause of the usage 'conjoined'; produced by the motion of one or both, or by another conjunction (VS 7.2.10 C).
The quality that destroys conjunction.
Spatial (far/near) and temporal (older/younger) qualities.
Quality grasped by sight alone; seven colours; in earth, water, fire.
Quality grasped by the tongue; six tastes; in earth and water.
Quality grasped by the nose; fragrant or not; in earth only.
Quality grasped by the skin alone; cold, hot, neither; in earth, water, fire, air.
Cause of the usage 'one' etc., from one up to parārdha; duality and higher numbers are non-eternal and produced by an enumerating cognition (apekṣābuddhi).

notes: Id disambiguated from the Sāṃkhya school ('sāṃkhya' → samkhya).

definitions.definition: The cognition 'this is one, this is one' that produces duality and higher numbers in things; its role at creation (for the magnitude of dyads) is one of Udayana's proofs of the Lord.
The cause in which the effect inheres (threads for cloth); a substance is an inherent cause (VS 1.1.14 C).
A cause inhering in the same thing as the effect or its cause (conjunction of threads for cloth; colour of threads for cloth's colour).
A cause other than the inherent and non-inherent (loom, weaver); the Lord is the efficient cause of the world.
Cause (kāraṇa): what invariably precedes an effect (and is not otherwise established); instrument (karaṇa): the special cause (Tarkasaṅgraha).
From the absence of the cause, absence of the effect, not vice versa (VS 1.2.1–2 C).
The effect is a new beginning, not pre-existing in its material cause (the whole produced by the parts is a new substance).

literal: doctrine that the effect does not pre-exist

definitions.definition: Before production the effect is non-existent (a prior absence of it is real) (NS 4.1.48–50; effect as counterpositive of prior absence, Tarkasaṅgraha).
A new substance over and above its parts, inhering in them and perceived (NS 2.1.31–37, 4.2.4–17).
The Vaiśeṣika view that when a clay pot is baked the pot dissolves into atoms, whose colour changes, and is then re-formed.
The Naiyāyika view that heat changes the colour of the pot as a whole without its dissolution.

A distinct self free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness, possessing merit, knowledge and concentration, who assists human effort and sets karma and the elements in motion; like a father to beings (NBh 4.1.21); the all-knowing maker of the world proved by inference (NK 5.1).
Maheśvara, by whose will the world is dissolved and created through the selves' adṛṣṭa (Praśastapāda).
The one omniscient supreme self with eternal cognition, desire and effort; author of the Veda; whose convention fixes word-meanings (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The name under which Praśastapāda's account of dissolution and creation speaks of the Lord.
The Lord, one and omniscient, as one of the two kinds of self (Tarkasaṅgraha).
'This supreme self is examined here' (NK 1.2).

notes: In Nyāya the supreme self is a distinct self, not the self of all.

definitions.definition: Distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Selves are many because of the distinctness of their states (VS 3.2.16 C).
Absolute release from pain (NS 1.1.22), reached when false knowledge and the rest are removed (NS 1.1.2); on the mainstream view without pleasure or cognition (NBh 1.1.22).

equivalents.note: Within Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, apavarga, mokṣa, mukti and niḥśreyasa (in its final sense) name the same state.
Sāṃkhya-Yoga's isolation of puruṣa is also a state without pain and without objects; but Nyāya's self is a substance whose consciousness is adventitious, while puruṣa is consciousness itself.

definitions.definition: Attained from knowledge of the truth of the sixteen categories (NS 1.1.1); in the science of the self it is the attainment of liberation (NBh 1.1.1).
One of the two results of dharma, beside prosperity (VS 1.1.2).
The first result of dharma (VS 1.1.2); sought through visible means where the visible result is absent, and through pure food with restraint (VS 6.1.8, 6.2.1, 6.2.9 C).
When adṛṣṭa is absent, no contact (with a body) and no new appearance (VS 5.2.20 C); quiescence like a fire whose fuel is burnt (Praśastapāda).
Absolute cessation of pain qualified by the experience of eternal pleasure (Bhāsarvajña — a minority view).
The absolute cessation of pain, i.e. a destruction of pain not contemporaneous with any prior absence of pain in the same self (Muktivāda).

Knowledge of the true nature of the categories — in the science of the self, of the self and the rest (NBh 1.1.1); it removes false knowledge (NS 1.1.2, 4.2.35) and arises from the practice of samādhi (NS 4.2.38).
Knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of the categories, arising from dharma (Praśastapāda).
The root of the series leading to pain (NS 1.1.2); its forms include 'there is no self', taking the non-self for the self, pain for pleasure, the impermanent for the permanent (NBh 1.1.2).

equivalents.note: Yoga's avidyā (YS 2.5) is likewise taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant and self; Nyāya's list overlaps but belongs to a different account of self.

definitions.definition: Characterized by impelling to activity (NS 1.1.18); three groups: attachment, aversion, delusion (NS 4.1.3).

notes: Homonym: in Āyurveda doṣa means the three humours.

definitions.definition: Attachment to the agreeable, arising from false knowledge (NBh 1.1.2); one of the three groups of faults.
Arises from pleasure, absorption, satisfaction, the unseen and particular birth (VS 6.2.12–16 C).
The worst of the faults, since the others arise only in the deluded (NS 4.1.6).
The undertaking of action by speech, mind and body (NS 1.1.17), good or bad (NBh 1.1.2).
Arising again (NS 1.1.19); established by the eternity of the self (NS 4.1.10).
The result produced by activity and faults (NS 1.1.20).
The substrate of purposive movement, senses and experienced objects (NS 1.1.11); earthy (NS 3.1.27).
Bodies of each element; some beings are not womb-born (VS 4.2.9 C; Tarkasaṅgraha).
Smell, taste, sight, touch, hearing, made from the elements (NS 1.1.12).
Each located in a bodily seat — nose-tip, tongue-tip, the black of the eye, the whole skin, the ear's ākāśa; manas is the inner sense.
The false notion of 'I' regarding body and the like, which ceases through knowledge of the truth about the causes of the faults (NS 4.2.1) and through contemplation of the body within (NBh 4.2.2).

notes: Not the Sāṃkhya evolute; here a mistaken cognition.

definitions.definition: The notion of the whole form (e.g. 'woman', 'man') with its embellishments that causes the faults (NS 4.2.3; NBh).
Viewing the body as hair, flesh, blood, bone, bile, excrement and so on, cultivated to abandon lustful passion (NBh 4.2.3).

cross_language.note: same term; the Buddhist practice has its own contexts and lists

definitions.definition: Repeated contemplation of objects (and then of the body) that removes false construction and the I-notion (NBh 4.2.2, 4.2.46).

The practice of a particular samādhi yields knowledge of truth (NS 4.2.38); obstacles to it are overcome by the continuing effect of prior practice (NS 4.2.41); Īśvara possesses concentration (NBh 4.1.21).
The state in which, the mind abiding in the self, the embodied one has no pleasure or pain (VS 5.2.17 C).
A means to liberation, practised in forests, caves and sandbanks, with the method of the inner self learned from the Yoga śāstra (NS 4.2.42, 4.2.46; NBh).
The means of dharma common to all life-stages (NBh 4.2.46).
Without restraint, pure food does not bring prosperity (VS 6.2.9 C).
The particular (means of dharma) for each life-stage (NBh 4.2.46).
Learned from the Yoga śāstra: austerity, breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, fixation (NBh 4.2.46).
The science of reasoning, the fourth of the four sciences, 'the lamp of all sciences' (NBh 1.1.1).
The examination of things by the means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1); also the five-membered demonstration.
Knowledge of the self as in the Upaniṣads; Nyāya is more than this because of its separate categories, though in it knowledge of truth is knowledge of the self (NBh 1.1.1).
Mīmāṃsā's claim that the Veda has no author, rejected by Nyāya: the Veda is composed with understanding and its validity comes from its reliable author.
Its authority follows from its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3).
The air moving within the body; one, named prāṇa, apāna and the rest by differences of adjunct (Tarkasaṅgraha); inhalation and exhalation are marks of the self (VS 3.2.4 C).
The region into which the mind enters in deep sleep, where, lacking contact with the skin-sense, it produces no cognition (commentarial tradition on the Muktāvalī).
Dreamless sleep, in which there is no affliction — the analogy by which liberation is shown possible (NS 4.1.63); explained as the mind's contact with purītat.
Dream cognition is like memory and imagination (NS 4.2.34); the notion of dream-objects is destroyed on waking (NS 4.2.35).
Arises, like memory, from self–mind conjunction and impressions (VS 9.23 C); a form of non-knowledge (Praśastapāda).
A quality of the self, the knower (NS 3.2.40), prompted by many causes (NS 3.2.41).
Cognition produced by impressions alone (Tarkasaṅgraha).

notes: Homonym: smṛti also names the class of remembered (non-Vedic) scriptures.

definitions.definition: Cognition other than memory; valid or invalid (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Knowledge of seers arising from particular merits (VS 9.28 C); intuitive knowledge of past, future and supersensible things in the seers (Praśastapāda).
The seers' kind of knowledge occasionally arising in ordinary people (Praśastapāda).
Arises from particular merits (VS 9.28 C).
Defective cognition arising from defects of the senses and from impressions (VS 9.25–26 C); doubt, error, indefinite cognition and dream (Praśastapāda).

notes: Not the cosmic ignorance of Advaita.

definitions.definition: Undefective cognition (VS 9.27 C): perception, inference, memory, seers' knowledge (Praśastapāda).
A form of non-knowledge — cognition that fails to determine its object ('what is this?') (Praśastapāda).
A fault of disposition; the life-stages yield merit according to its absence (VS 6.2.3–5 C).
The periodic origination of the world, initiated by Maheśvara's desire to create, through motion in atoms caused by the selves' adṛṣṭa (Praśastapāda).
The periodic dissolution of all products into atoms at the end of a Brahmā's lifespan by Maheśvara's desire (Praśastapāda).
Division of wholes does not end in nothingness, because atoms exist (NS 4.2.16).
Beings (bodies) not born from wombs exist, also on the evidence of the Veda (VS 4.2.9 C).
Not a substance but merely the absence of light (VS 5.2.21 C).

notes: Homonym: distinct from the Sāṃkhya guṇa tamas.

definitions.definition: The three debts with which, according to scripture, a brāhmaṇa is born; urged as a bar to liberation and answered as figurative (NS 4.1.59–62; NBh).

literal: receiving (the fruit of) what was not done

definitions.definition: The absurdity of reaping results of acts one did not do — used to refute rival accounts of embodiment and of the agent (NS 3.2.38, 3.2.72 DCS).
Six conditions that disqualify a property from being a genuine universal (Udayana).
The property (or relation) by which a property or relation is specified — e.g. potness delimits the counterpositiveness of 'absence of pot'.
That of which something is the absence (the pot, for 'absence of pot'), or the first term of a relation.
The locus in which a relation or absence is (the ground, for 'absence of pot on the ground').
What appears in a cognition as qualifying something; its property is prakāratā.
What a cognition is about as qualified; its property is viśeṣyatā.
A property qualifying a thing; the qualifier–qualified relation (viśeṣaṇatā) is the contact by which absence is perceived.
The relation by which the qualifier is cognized as linked to the qualificand; its property is saṃsargatā.
The property of being the content of a cognition, analysed into qualificandness, qualifierness and relationness.
The correlation of relational properties that define each other (e.g. causehood determined by effecthood).
A relation by which one thing can occur in another (e.g. conjunction, inherence), as opposed to relations that do not ground occurrence.
A relation that is nothing over and above its relata, e.g. that of absence to its locus.
The relation by which a number such as 'two' resides in both relata together, not in each singly.
A property that occurs in a locus only in part (e.g. monkey-contact in a tree), coexisting with its own absence — a test case for definitions of pervasion.
Occurring in the same locus; pervasion is a kind of co-location of probans and probandum.
The principle preferring the simpler definition or explanation.
The cognition produced by consideration (parāmarśa).
Its presence makes inference possible even of what is already known (Gaṅgeśa's definition of pakṣatā).
A pseudo-reason whose probandum's absence is known by another means of knowledge ('fire is not hot').
A reason faced by another reason proving the absence of the probandum.
Three kinds: as to the locus (the sky-lotus), as to itself, as to pervasion (with an adjunct).
A reason that strays from the probandum; common, uncommon, non-conclusive.
A reason pervaded by the absence of the probandum ('sound is eternal because produced').
A pseudo-reason in the Nyāya Sūtra's list (NS 1.2.7 DCS).
A pseudo-reason that itself needs proof (NS 1.2.8 DCS).
A pseudo-reason adduced when its time has passed (NS 1.2.9 DCS).
Extraordinary contact in which a prior cognition presents its object (e.g. fragrance in 'fragrant sandal' seen); used to explain some errors.
Extraordinary contact by which all instances of a universal (all smoke) are grasped, grounding knowledge of pervasion.
The sixth ordinary contact, by which absence and inherence are perceived.
The complete set of causal conditions, including the absence of counteragents, which suffices for an effect (no separate causal power needed).
What prevents an effect when present (e.g. a gem or mantra stopping fire's burning); its absence is a cause.
An invariable antecedent that is nevertheless not a cause (e.g. the colour of the potter's staff).
The relation in which a qualifier stands to what it qualifies — in perception, the contact for absence.
